questions.prompt: A browser task logs A, schedules `Promise.resolve().then(()=>log("B"))`, schedules a timer to log C, then logs D. What order follows?

choices.text: A, C, B, D because scheduling a timer pauses the current task.
A, D, B, C under the ordinary browser task and microtask model.
A, B, D, C because a resolved promise reaction runs synchronously.
A, D, C, B because timers always run before every microtask.

questions.explanation: The task completes A then D. The microtask checkpoint runs the Promise reaction B before the timer task C. Scheduling does not pause the current task.

questions.prompt: A then handler returns 42 without throwing. What happens to the promise returned by then?

choices.text: It fulfills with 42 as the handler result.
It always fulfills with the original promise value regardless of the return.
It rejects because a then handler must return another promise object.
It stays pending because primitive return values are ignored by chaining.

questions.explanation: A reaction return value fulfills the derived promise, with promise resolution adopting thenables when applicable. A primitive return is valid.

questions.prompt: Two promises passed to Promise.all resolve in the reverse order from the input. What ordering does its result array use?

choices.text: Completion order, even when it differs from the input order.
Sorted order based on the string form of each resolved value.
Unspecified order because parallel promises cannot retain their indices.
Input order, even when completion order differs.

questions.explanation: Promise.all associates results with input indices. Completion order does not determine the final array order.

questions.prompt: A microtask recursively queues another microtask without ending. Why can browser painting be delayed?

choices.text: Microtasks always move to a separate worker and cannot delay the window event loop.
Rendering interrupts every callback after one statement to keep the screen current.
The checkpoint can keep draining queued microtasks before a rendering opportunity.
Every microtask is guaranteed a new visible paint before the next one runs.

questions.explanation: A microtask checkpoint drains work until the queue is empty. Continually adding work can delay progressing to other event-loop work and rendering.

questions.prompt: A Promise constructor executor logs E; its then handler logs T; the current task later logs S. What is the relevant timing distinction?

choices.text: Both always run synchronously before any code after the constructor.
The executor runs during construction; the reaction waits until its job runs.
Both executor and reaction are deferred to the same future timer task.
The executor is deferred but the reaction runs during then registration.

questions.explanation: Promise construction invokes the executor immediately. Promise reactions are queued jobs rather than synchronous calls during then registration.
